The elementary charge, usually denoted by e, is a fundamental physical constant, defined as the electric charge carried by a single proton (+1 e) or, equivalently, the magnitude of the negative electric charge carried by a single electron, which has charge −1 e.

The Boltzmann constant (kB or k) is the proportionality factor that relates the average relative thermal energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas.

the exchange rate at which one unit of a currency buys the same basket of goods in two countries
An exchange rate is the rate at which one currency will be exchanged for another. It is also regarded as the value of one country's currency in relation to another currency.
The amount of money being converted from the source currency, expressed in units of that source currency.
The amount of money produced by the conversion, expressed in units of the target currency.
The currency from which an amount is converted in a currency-conversion operation.
The currency into which an amount is converted in a currency-conversion operation.
The process of changing an amount of money from one currency into the equivalent amount in another currency at the prevailing exchange rate.
The bid price is the highest price a buyer (typically a market maker) is willing to pay for a currency at a given moment.
The ask price (also called the offer price) is the lowest price a seller (typically a market maker) is willing to accept for a currency at a given moment.

The bid-ask spread is the difference between the ask price and the bid price for a given currency or other asset. It represents the implicit transaction cost of trading and is a key indicator of market liquidity.
The bid-ask spread expressed as a percentage of the ask price, allowing direct comparison of spreads across different currencies and price levels.
A change expressed as a fraction of the original value times 100. Standard formula: (new − old) / old × 100.

The interest rate is the proportion of a loan or deposit that is charged or paid as interest, typically expressed as an annual percentage. Central bank policy rates are key drivers of currency valuations and forward rates.
A ranking is always defined relative to one or more criteria that determine the order. For currencies, common criteria include trading turnover, reserve holdings, and market capitalisation.
The superlative form of relevance, used to identify the items deemed most important within a given set according to chosen criteria.
Trading turnover is the total volume of trades executed in a market over a specified period. For foreign exchange, it is typically measured in USD-equivalent value.
Turnover figures are often reported as averages (typically arithmetic means) over a defined period to give a representative value rather than a one-off snapshot.

A cross rate is an exchange rate between two currencies, neither of which is the official currency of the country in which the quote is given. More generally, it is a rate derived from each currency's rate against a common third currency such as the US dollar.
The movement in an exchange rate between two points in time, expressed either in absolute terms or as a percentage.
The earlier of two exchange rate observations, used as the baseline in computing a rate change.
The more recent of two exchange rate observations, compared against the old rate to compute a rate change.

A forward exchange rate is the rate at which a bank agrees today to exchange one currency for another at a specified future date. Forward rates are derived from spot rates and interest rate differentials via the covered interest parity relationship.
The spot rate is the current exchange rate at which a currency pair can be bought or sold for immediate delivery (typically T+2 settlement).
The interest rate applicable to the base currency of a currency pair. Higher base-currency interest rates relative to the quote currency typically lead to forward rates below spot.
The interest rate applicable to the quote currency of a currency pair. Higher quote-currency interest rates relative to the base currency typically lead to forward rates above spot.
Daily turnover aggregates all trades executed within a single trading day.
Weekly turnover aggregates daily turnover figures across a calendar week.
Yearly turnover aggregates trading activity across a calendar or fiscal year, providing a long-term view of market activity.
Daily average turnover expresses turnover as a per-day mean, calculated by dividing total turnover in a period by the number of trading days.
Monthly average turnover expresses turnover as a per-month mean over a longer reporting horizon.
Yearly average turnover expresses turnover as a per-year mean, typically derived from monthly averages.
A ranking that uses daily turnover as the ordering criterion to compare currencies, exchanges, or instruments.
A ranking that uses weekly turnover as the ordering criterion.
A ranking that uses yearly turnover as the ordering criterion. This is typically considered the most stable and relevant criterion for ranking currencies.
Yearly turnover ranking is treated here as the canonical 'most relevant' ranking for currencies, as it smooths out short-term volatility.
Weekly turnover ranking provides a mid-term view of currency relevance, balancing immediacy with stability.
Daily turnover ranking gives the most immediate view of currency relevance but is more volatile than longer-term rankings.

The United States dollar (symbol: $; currency code: USD) is the official currency of the United States and several other countries. It is the world's primary reserve currency and the most-traded currency on the foreign exchange market. The dollar is divided into 100 cents.

The United States dollar (symbol: $; currency code: USD) is the official currency of the United States and several other countries. It is the world's primary reserve currency and the most-traded currency on the foreign exchange market. The dollar is divided into 100 cents.

The Australian dollar (symbol: $ or A$; currency code: AUD) is the official currency of the Commonwealth of Australia, including its external territories, as well as the independent Pacific states of Kiribati, Nauru, and Tuvalu. It is divided into 100 cents and was introduced in 1966, replacing the Australian pound.

The Canadian dollar (symbol: $ or C$; currency code: CAD) is the official currency of Canada. It is issued by the Bank of Canada and is one of the world's most-traded currencies. The Canadian dollar is divided into 100 cents and is often regarded as a commodity currency due to Canada's substantial natural-resource exports.

The Hong Kong dollar (symbol: HK$; currency code: HKD) is the official currency of Hong Kong. It is divided into 100 cents and has been pegged to the United States dollar since 1983 at a rate of approximately 7.80 HKD per USD. It is issued by three commercial note-issuing banks under the authority of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.

The Singapore dollar (symbol: S$; currency code: SGD) is the official currency of Singapore. It is divided into 100 cents and is issued by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. It is interchangeable with the Brunei dollar at par under a Currency Interchangeability Agreement.

The New Zealand dollar (symbol: NZ$; currency code: NZD) is the official currency of New Zealand and several Pacific island states (Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Pitcairn Islands). It is divided into 100 cents and is informally known as the 'Kiwi dollar'. It is issued by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.

The Swiss franc (symbol: Fr. or CHF; currency code: CHF) is the official currency and legal tender of Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and is also used in the Italian exclave of Campione d'Italia. Issued by the Swiss National Bank, it is widely regarded as a safe-haven currency due to Switzerland's political stability and low inflation.

The Japanese yen (symbol: ¥; currency code: JPY) is the official currency of Japan, issued by the Bank of Japan. It is the third most-traded currency in the world after the US dollar and the euro, and serves as a major global reserve currency.

The Swedish krona (symbol: kr; currency code: SEK) is the official currency of Sweden. It is divided into 100 öre and is issued by the Sveriges Riksbank, the central bank of Sweden. The plural form in Swedish is kronor.

The Danish krone (symbol: kr; currency code: DKK) is the official currency of Denmark, Greenland, and the Faroe Islands. It is divided into 100 øre and is issued by Danmarks Nationalbank. The krone is pegged to the euro through the European Exchange Rate Mechanism II.

The Norwegian krone (symbol: kr; currency code: NOK) is the official currency of Norway and its dependent territories. It is divided into 100 øre and is issued by Norges Bank, the central bank of Norway. The plural form in Norwegian is kroner.

The South Korean won (symbol: ₩; currency code: KRW) is the official currency of South Korea. It is issued by the Bank of Korea. Although a subunit called the jeon exists in theory (1/100 of a won), it is not used in everyday transactions due to its negligible value.

The Indian rupee (symbol: ₹; currency code: INR) is the official currency of India. It is divided into 100 paise (singular: paisa) and is issued by the Reserve Bank of India. The rupee symbol ₹ was officially adopted in 2010.

The Mexican peso (symbol: $ or MX$; currency code: MXN) is the official currency of Mexico. It is divided into 100 centavos and is issued by the Banco de México. The peso is one of the most-traded currencies in Latin America and serves as a common proxy for emerging-market sentiment.

The Chilean peso (symbol: $ or CLP$; currency code: CLP) is the official currency of Chile. It is issued by the Central Bank of Chile. The peso is divided in theory into 100 centavos, but centavos are no longer used due to their negligible value.

The Philippine peso (symbol: ₱; currency code: PHP) is the official currency of the Philippines. It is divided into 100 sentimos (also called centavos) and is issued by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. The peso symbol ₱ was officially adopted in 1967.

The Colombian peso (symbol: $ or COL$; currency code: COP) is the official currency of Colombia. It is divided into 100 centavos and is issued by the Banco de la República. Centavos are no longer used in practice due to their negligible value.

The Argentine peso (symbol: $ or ARG$; currency code: ARS) is the official currency of Argentina. It is divided into 100 centavos and is issued by the Central Bank of Argentina (Banco Central de la República Argentina). It is one of the most volatile major currencies, having been subject to repeated devaluations.

The South African rand (symbol: R; currency code: ZAR) is the official currency of South Africa and is also legal tender in the Common Monetary Area together with the currencies of Lesotho, Namibia, and Eswatini. It is divided into 100 cents and is issued by the South African Reserve Bank.

The Brazilian real (symbol: R$; currency code: BRL) is the official currency of Brazil. It is divided into 100 centavos and is issued by the Banco Central do Brasil. The current real was introduced in 1994 as part of the Plano Real economic stabilisation program.

The Polish złoty (symbol: zł; currency code: PLN) is the official currency of Poland. It is divided into 100 groszy (singular: grosz) and is issued by the Narodowy Bank Polski. The word 'złoty' is the masculine form of the Polish adjective meaning 'golden'.

The Thai baht (symbol: ฿; currency code: THB) is the official currency of Thailand. It is divided into 100 satang and is issued by the Bank of Thailand. The baht traces its origins to a traditional unit of weight used for measuring silver.

The Indonesian rupiah (symbol: Rp; currency code: IDR) is the official currency of Indonesia. It is issued by Bank Indonesia, the central bank. The rupiah is one of the most heavily denominated currencies in the world, with banknotes commonly ranging up to 100,000 rupiah.

The Czech koruna (symbol: Kč; currency code: CZK) is the official currency of the Czech Republic. It is divided into 100 haléř (singular: haléř), although hellers are no longer in circulation. It is issued by the Czech National Bank. The word 'koruna' means 'crown'.

The Turkish lira (symbol: ₺; currency code: TRY) is the official currency of Turkey and Northern Cyprus. It is divided into 100 kuruş and is issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. The current lira replaced the old lira in 2005 at a ratio of 1,000,000 old lira to 1 new lira.

The Hungarian forint (symbol: Ft; currency code: HUF) is the official currency of Hungary. It was historically divided into 100 fillér, although fillér coins are no longer in use. It is issued by the Hungarian National Bank (Magyar Nemzeti Bank).

The Saudi riyal (symbol: ﷼; currency code: SAR) is the official currency of Saudi Arabia. It is divided into 100 halalas and is issued by the Saudi Central Bank. The riyal has been pegged to the US dollar since 1986 at a rate of 3.75 SAR per USD.

The Malaysian ringgit (symbol: RM; currency code: MYR) is the official currency of Malaysia. It is divided into 100 sen and is issued by Bank Negara Malaysia, the country's central bank. The word 'ringgit' originally meant 'jagged' in Malay, referring to the milled edges of Spanish silver dollars used in colonial-era trade.

The Russian ruble (symbol: ₽; currency code: RUB) is the official currency of the Russian Federation. It is divided into 100 kopecks and is issued by the Central Bank of Russia. The ruble is one of the world's oldest national currencies, with origins traced to the 13th century.

The Romanian leu (symbol: L; currency code: RON) is the official currency of Romania. It is divided into 100 bani (singular: ban) and is issued by the National Bank of Romania. The word 'leu' is Romanian for 'lion'. The current leu was introduced in 2005 to replace the old leu at a ratio of 10,000 to 1.

The Peruvian sol (symbol: S/; currency code: PEN) is the official currency of Peru. It is divided into 100 céntimos and is issued by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru. The current sol replaced the nuevo sol in 2015, though it has the same value.

The Bahraini dinar (symbol: .د.ب; currency code: BHD) is the official currency of Bahrain. It is divided into 1,000 fils and is issued by the Central Bank of Bahrain. The dinar has been pegged to the US dollar since 2001 at a rate of approximately 0.376 BHD per USD.

The Bulgarian lev (currency code: BGN) is the official currency of Bulgaria. It is divided into 100 stotinki and is issued by the Bulgarian National Bank. The lev has been pegged to the euro since 1999 as part of a currency board arrangement.

The United Arab Emirates dirham (symbol: د.إ; currency code: AED) is the official currency of the United Arab Emirates. It is divided into 100 fils and is issued by the Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates. It has been pegged to the US dollar since 1997.

Pound sterling (symbol: £; currency code: GBP) is the official currency of the United Kingdom and several British overseas territories and Crown Dependencies. It is the oldest currency still in continuous use and the fourth most-traded currency on the foreign exchange market. One pound is divided into 100 pence.

Replacing coal-fired power and heat with low-carbon generation. Largest single fossil emission source. Overlaps strongly with solar energy and wind energy; potentials must not be summed. Translation of the German keyword 'Kohleausstieg'.

Cutting CH4 from oil, gas, coal, waste and agriculture. UNEP/CCAC: up to 45 percent (180 Mt CH4/yr, about 5 Gt CO2eq at GWP100) by 2030, avoiding about 0.3 degree C by the 2040s; majority of measures at low or negative cost. Translation of the German keyword 'Methanreduktion'.
Cross-sector efficiency in industry, buildings, appliances and processes. IEA calls it the first fuel; most measures have negative lifetime cost. Translation of the German keyword 'Energieeffizienz'.
Deep energy retrofits of the existing building stock (insulation, windows, heating systems). High potential but chronically low renovation rates. Translation of the German keyword 'Gebäudesanierung'.
Replacing fossil heating boilers with electric heat pumps in buildings and low-temperature industry. Translation of the German keyword 'Wärmepumpen'.
Decarbonized heat networks using waste heat, large heat pumps, geothermal and thermal storage in dense areas. Translation of the German keyword 'Fernwärme'.
Utility-scale and rooftop photovoltaics. Largest and cheapest 2030 potential in IPCC AR6 Figure SPM.7; deployment already on a steep growth track. Translation of the German keyword 'Solarenergie'.
Onshore and offshore wind power. Second largest low-cost 2030 potential in IPCC AR6 Figure SPM.7. Translation of the German keyword 'Windenergie'.
New nuclear plants and lifetime extensions. Low-carbon but slow to build; near-term potential limited by construction times. Translation of the German keyword 'Kernenergie'.
Geothermal electricity and direct heat use, including emerging deep and enhanced systems. Translation of the German keyword 'Geothermie'.

Batteries, pumped hydro and long-duration storage. Enabler that unlocks variable renewables rather than a direct emission cut; potential counted as enabled reduction. Translation of the German keyword 'Energiespeicher'.
Transmission and distribution build-out plus interconnectors. Enabler for renewables integration; potential counted as enabled reduction. Translation of the German keyword 'Netzausbau'.
General motorway speed limits. Tiny global potential (Germany alone below 0.01 Gt/yr) but near-zero setup cost. Translation of the German keyword 'Tempolimit'.

Per-capita refund of carbon price revenue. Direct effect small; main value is raising public acceptance and thus the fulfillment probability of carbon pricing. Translation of the German keyword 'Klimageld'.
A duty levied on goods when they cross a customs border.
Cap-and-trade systems with declining caps (EU ETS and successors). Overlaps with carbon price; proven instrument. Translation of the German keyword 'Emissionshandel'.
Battery-electric passenger vehicles plus charging infrastructure. Strong market momentum. Translation of the German keyword 'Elektromobilität'.
Electric and efficient trucks, rail modal shift and logistics optimization for goods transport. Translation of the German keyword 'Güterverkehr'.

System-wide reuse, remanufacturing and product life extension reducing primary material demand. Overlaps with recycling and material efficiency. Translation of the German keyword 'Kreislaufwirtschaft'.
Lightweight design, higher material yields and substitution (e.g. low-clinker cement, timber construction). Translation of the German keyword 'Materialeffizienz'.
Rewetting drained peatlands, which currently emit on the order of 1 to 2 Gt CO2eq/yr globally. Translation of the German keyword 'Wiedervernässung'.
Organic carbon stored in the soil.
Separating CO2 from a gas stream so that it can be stored or used.

Electrolytic hydrogen for steel, chemicals, shipping and long-term storage. Limited to hard-to-electrify uses; expectations corrected downward since 2023. Translation of the German keyword 'Grüner Wasserstoff'.
Improved nutrient management, rice cultivation, livestock feeding and manure handling reducing N2O and CH4. Translation of the German keyword 'Nachhaltige Landwirtschaft'.
The amount of meat eaten.
Food that is lost or thrown away along the supply chain.
Greenhouse gas released by air traffic.
Binding CO2 and efficiency standards for vehicles, appliances and buildings. Regulation is cheap to set up and has a strong track record. Translation of the German keyword 'CO₂-Standards'.
Concessional finance and de-risking for mitigation in developing countries; enabler whose potential is the reduction it unlocks. Translation of the German keyword 'Klimafinanzierung'.
The chain of suppliers that contribute to a final product.

Due diligence and disclosure duties pushing emission cuts through corporate supply chains. Translation of the German keyword 'Lieferkettengesetze'.
